name: Ylang-ylang oil (Cananga odorata)
short: On skin: contact allergy; commonest positive essential-oil patch test (3.1-3.9%) in dermatitis clinics; occupational case reports. Healthy volunteers, inhaled or on skin: blood pressure fell.
text: The main documented harm is allergic skin reactions. In a large central European dermatology network, among 15,682 patients patch tested with at least one essential oil from 2000 to 2008, ylang-ylang oil was the most common positive reaction (a weighted mean of 3.1% positive tests), and among 10,930 patients tested from 2010 to 2019 it again had the highest rate of positive reactions (3.9%); these were patients already attending skin clinics, and the later study found that sensitisation to essential oils occurs albeit infrequently in most cases, with masseurs and cosmeticians at increased risk. Two case reports are titled “Occupational allergic contact dermatitis caused by ylang-ylang oil” and “Occupational contact dermatitis from ylang-ylang oil” (no abstracts are available). A safety review of ylang-ylang oil as a food flavouring states that it has been reported to cause skin sensitisation in animals and humans, but found no indication that food exposure has caused allergic reactions, and noted that the only inhalation toxicity study, which tested it as part of a larger fragrance mixture, gave no indication of adverse effects but is likely of minimal relevance to oral food-flavouring use. In small studies in healthy volunteers, inhaling ylang-ylang oil (24 people; 29 men) or absorbing it through the skin (40 people) lowered blood pressure and, in the inhalation studies, pulse or heart rate; the abstracts do not report adverse events. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
